provenance.other: “voice of the people” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Adjudicated at Mosiah 7:9 and again at Mosiah 29:2, where the phrase returns to answer the passage it first translated; written here because Helaman is a new book (ADJUDICATING §4).
provenance.significance: 1 Samuel 8:7 is God telling Samuel to hearken unto the voice of the people because it is not Samuel they have rejected but God. Mosiah 29 used the phrase to found the reign of the judges on that voice, with the explicit assurance that it is not common for the voice of the people to desire anything contrary to right. Helaman 5:2 is the sentence in which that assurance fails: 'as their laws and their governments were established by the voice of the people, and they which chose evil were more numerous than they which chose good, therefore they were ripening for destruction.' Recover 1 Samuel and the collapse is not a surprise — the KJV's one verse about the voice of the people is a verse in which that voice is a rejection of God, and Mosiah's constitution was built on it.

5:2.note: The clause names the Mosiah constitution by the phrase Mosiah 29 founded it on, and it names it in the sentence that pronounces its failure. This is the third stage of a single argument the Book of Mormon conducts across three books: 1 Samuel's warning, Mosiah's qualified adoption, Helaman's verdict. The link is written rather than filed as a recurrence because a reader of Helaman meets the phrase in a new hand and a new book, and because what is new is the arithmetic — the voice of the people is here a majority, counted, and wrong.
5:2.text: And the LORD said unto Samuel, Hearken unto the voice of the people in all that they say unto thee: for they have not rejected thee, but they have rejected me, that I should not reign over them.

provenance.other: “lay up for yourselves” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 6:20, whose object is 'treasures in heaven'. Helaman has the singular, 'a treasure in Heaven'. “fadeth not away” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, 1 Peter 1:4 (an inheritance 'reserved in heaven for you') and 1 Peter 5:4 (a crown of glory).
provenance.significance: Matthew 6 is the KJV's one sustained argument that a good work done to be seen loses its reward, and the treasure saying is its conclusion. Helaman 5:8 reproduces the argument's structure before it reproduces its words: 'that ye may not do these things that ye may boast, but that ye may do these things to lay up for yourselves a treasure in Heaven'. That is Matthew 6:1's condition ('do not your alms before men, to be seen of them: otherwise ye have no reward') attached to Matthew 6:20's clause. The metalepsis is in what Helaman leaves out: Matthew's reason for the heavenly treasure is that moth and rust corrupt the earthly one, and Helaman replaces it with 1 Peter's incorruptible inheritance — the same doctrine, from the epistle that supplies this chapter's other borrowing at 5:44.

5:8.note: 'To lay up for yourselves a treasure in Heaven, yea, which is eternal, and which fadeth not away.' A KJV singleton in its exact form, with the number of the noun changed, followed immediately by a two-verse Petrine phrase that supplies the reason Matthew gave differently. Helaman's warning against doing good in order to boast is Matthew 6's own frame, and it arrives four verses before 5:12 puts the chapter's other Sermon-on-the-Mount borrowing to work.
5:8.text: But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust doth corrupt, and where thieves do not break through nor steal:

provenance.other: “beat upon” occurs in exactly three KJV verses: Jonah 4:8, where the sun beats on Jonah's head, and Matthew 7:25 and 7:27, which are the two halves of the house-on-the-rock parable. Luke's version of the parable (6:48) reads 'the stream beat vehemently upon that house' and has 'laid the foundation on a rock', which is nearer Helaman's 'build your foundation' than Matthew's 'founded upon a rock'; but Luke lacks the winds, and Helaman has them.
provenance.significance: Matthew's parable has four elements in a fixed order — the rock, the building, the storm beating upon the house, the not-falling — and Helaman 5:12 has all four in that order with one substitution: the storm has an author. 'When the Devil shall send forth his mighty winds; yea, his shafts in the whirlwind; yea, when all his hail and his mighty storm shall beat upon you.' Matthew's weather is impersonal and is simply what happens to every house; Helaman's is assault by a named adversary, which converts a parable about hearing and doing into a parable about temptation. What survives the change is Matthew's grammar: the storm still beats upon, and the house still does not fall.

5:12.note: The chapter's best-known verse and a genuine extended allusion rather than a quotation — no clause of Matthew is reproduced whole. What is reproduced is the parable's sequence and its one rare verb. Helaman also inverts the parable's frame: Matthew builds on the rock of hearing Christ's sayings, Helaman on 'the rock of our Redeemer, which is Christ, the Son of God', which makes the rock a person. The 1830's 'a foundation whereon if men buildeth, they cannot fall' keeps the parable's own consequence clause.
5:12.text: And the rain descended, and the floods came, and the winds blew, and beat upon that house; and it fell not: for it was founded upon a rock.

provenance.other: “sure foundation” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Isaiah 28:16 is quoted twice in the New Testament, at Romans 9:33 and 1 Peter 2:6, and mediation-check.py run against 1 Peter 2:6 returns one genuinely decisive point: the Book of Mormon has Isaiah's 'a sure foundation', which neither New Testament form contains — 1 Peter reads 'a chief corner stone, elect, precious'. (The tool reports a second decisive point on 'foundation a stone a tried stone a precious'; that one is an artefact of the single shared word 'foundation' and is not counted here.) Against Romans 9:33 the tool finds no decisive divergence at all, which is expected — Romans is the shorter of the two quotations.
provenance.significance: Isaiah 28:16 is the KJV's foundation-stone verse and the New Testament made it a christological proof text, so a nineteenth-century writer reaching for a rock-and-foundation image had two forms available. Helaman took the Old Testament one. That matters because the phrase he took is precisely the phrase the apostles dropped: 'a sure foundation' is the half of Isaiah's oracle that speaks of the building rather than of the stone's preciousness, and it is the half Helaman's argument needs, since his sentence is about whether a structure will stand. The verse fuses it with Matthew 7's parable, so the Old Testament supplies the foundation and the New Testament the storm.

5:12.note: Two words, but a KJV singleton, and the mediation test makes the finding: 'a sure foundation' survives in neither apostolic quotation of Isaiah 28:16, so the Book of Mormon has the Old Testament form of a verse it would have been far easier to reach through Romans or 1 Peter. Held at high rather than certain because two words is a slender basis for a route claim; what supports it is that the words are the ones the mediators discarded.
5:12.text: Therefore thus saith the Lord GOD, Behold, I lay in Zion for a foundation a stone, a tried stone, a precious corner stone, a sure foundation: he that believeth shall not make haste.

provenance.other: “what ye shall speak” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 10:19 and Mark 13:11, and only Matthew puts the giving and the speaking in one clause: 'it shall be given you in that same hour what ye shall speak'. Mark separates them ('whatsoever shall be given you in that hour, that speak ye') and Luke 12:12 replaces speaking with 'what ye ought to say'. mediation-check.py run on Matthew against Mark returns a single decisive point, and it is an absence — the Book of Mormon lacks Mark's 'but the Holy Ghost' — which is weak evidence on its own. The construction is the better discriminator: Helaman 5:18's 'they also had what they should speak, given unto them' is Matthew's clause with the participle moved to the end.
provenance.significance: Matthew 10:19 is spoken to disciples about to be delivered up to councils and scourged in synagogues, and its promise is for what to say when arrested. Helaman 5:18 gives the promise three verses before the arrest: 'they had power and authority given unto them that they might speak; and they also had what they should speak, given unto them' — and at 5:21 Nephi and Lehi are taken by an army and cast into prison. The chapter is running Matthew 10's own sequence, and the borrowed clause is the one that tells the reader what the imprisonment is for.

5:18.note: 'And they also had what they should speak, given unto them.' Matthew's two-verse phrase with Matthew's participle, in an English that reads oddly precisely because it is holding two KJV elements in one clause. Filed as an allusion rather than a quotation because nothing is reproduced whole; the argument rests on the construction and on the arrest that follows it.
5:18.text: But when they deliver you up, take no thought how or what ye shall speak: for it shall be given you in that same hour what ye shall speak.

provenance.other: “in the midst of the fire” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Daniel 3:25, but the Book of Mormon reads 'in the midst of fire' without the article, so the singleton is not claimable as verbal contact and the link is filed as figural. Daniel 3:22 has the flame slaying the men who came near; Daniel 3:27 has bodies the fire had no power over, not a hair singed, no smell of fire.
provenance.significance: Daniel 3 is the KJV's only episode in which men stand unharmed inside fire while the people who came to destroy them are the ones endangered by it, and Helaman 5:23-25 reproduces both halves: Nephi and Lehi are not burned, and the Lamanites 'durst not lay their hands upon them for fear, lest they should be burned'. Daniel's fourth figure in the furnace, 'like the Son of God', has a counterpart at 5:36-39, where the prisoners are seen conversing with beings whose faces are not their own. What the Book of Mormon adds is the direction of the fire: in Daniel it is the king's furnace and God protects men from it, here it is God's fire and it is the executioners who are held off by it.

5:23.note: No clause is shared and the one candidate singleton fails on an article, so this is written as figural under CONVENTIONS §2 and §0a rather than argued as verbal dependence. What justifies it is that the KJV has exactly one fire that does not burn the righteous, and this chapter builds a whole episode on the premise. The pillar of fire at 5:43 is a separate and older image and is excluded rather than fused in.
5:23.whyNot: Two ordinary words, and the article that would have made the phrase a singleton is absent. A writer describing a miraculous fire in nineteenth-century English would produce this vocabulary with or without Daniel 3, and no distinctive element of Daniel's story — the furnace, the three names, the fourth man, the unsinged hair — appears in the Book of Mormon text.
5:23.text: He answered and said, Lo, I see four men loose, walking in the midst of the fire, and they have no hurt; and the form of the fourth is like the Son of God.

provenance.other: “foundations of the prison” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Acts 16:26 is the KJV's one prison earthquake: 'suddenly there was a great earthquake, so that the foundations of the prison were shaken'. The Book of Mormon has already used it twice, at Mosiah 7:8 and at Alma 14:27, where the prison walls actually fall; Helaman 5:27 is the one place the walls shake and do not fall — 'as if they were about to tumble to the earth; but behold, they did not fall'.
provenance.significance: Acts 16 supplies the whole shape of Helaman 5:21-44: preachers imprisoned, an earthquake at midnight, the jailers in terror, the question 'what must I do to be saved', and a conversion inside the prison. Helaman answers Acts point by point and changes one thing. In Acts the earthquake opens the doors and looses the bands, and the jailer is converted by finding the prisoners still there; in Helaman the walls are explicitly not opened — the fire 'neither did it take hold upon the walls of the prison' (5:44) — and the deliverance is a cloud, a voice and a light rather than an escape. Recover Acts and the refusal is the point: this prison is not being opened, because the people who need delivering are inside it with the preachers.

5:27.note: The chapter's structural debt is to Acts 16 and 5:27 is where the wording touches it. Written here rather than carried from Alma 14:27 because Helaman is a new book (ADJUDICATING §4) and because the borrowing is inverted: Alma's prison falls, this one shakes and stands. That difference is the argument, and it runs through to 5:40's 'What shall we do'.
5:27.text: And suddenly there was a great earthquake, so that the foundations of the prison were shaken: and immediately all the doors were opened, and every one’s bands were loosed.

provenance.other: “still small voice” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The Book of Mormon reads 'a still voice, of perfect mildness, as if it had been a whisper', dropping 'small' and glossing it twice. At 5:46 the formula returns as 'a pleasant voice, as if it were a whisper', and the n-gram stream matched that verse to 1 Kings 19:13, 'there came a voice unto him' — which is the next verse of the same episode.
provenance.significance: 1 Kings 19:11-12 is a sequence and Helaman 5:27-33 runs it backwards. Elijah gets wind, then earthquake, then fire, and the LORD is in none of them; then the still small voice, and that is God. Helaman gives the earthquake first (5:27), then the cloud of darkness, then the voice — and the voice is expressly measured against the alternatives Elijah was given: 'it was not a voice of thunder; neither was it a voice of a great tumultuous noise; but behold, it was a still voice'. The negations are the borrowing. Then Helaman does something 1 Kings does not: the earth shakes again while the mild voice is speaking (5:31), so the two are simultaneous rather than sequential, and the point of Elijah's theophany — that God is not in the earthquake — is quietly denied. The voice is mild and the earth shakes anyway.

5:30.note: A KJV singleton, glossed rather than quoted, inside a theophany that reproduces 1 Kings 19's own list of what the voice is not. Adjudicated at 1 Nephi 17:45; written again here because Helaman is a new book (ADJUDICATING §4) and because this is the passage that argues with its source. 5:46's second 'as if it were a whisper' is Mormon reusing his own gloss and is registered as a recurrence.
5:30.text: And after the earthquake a fire; but the LORD was not in the fire: and after the fire a still small voice.

provenance.other: “Repent ye: for the kingdom” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. “the kingdom of heaven is at hand” occurs in exactly three: Matthew 3:2 (John the Baptist), 4:17 (Jesus, with the singular 'Repent'), and 10:7 (the twelve, without the imperative). Only Matthew 3:2 has the plural imperative the Book of Mormon has.
provenance.significance: The whole of Matthew 3:2 is eight words and Helaman 5:32 reproduces all of them, which puts it well below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold for a quotation and above any reasonable doubt about dependence — the verse simply has no more words to reproduce. What the borrowing carries with it is the speaker: Matthew 3:2 is John the Baptist's whole recorded preaching, delivered in a wilderness to a people going out to be baptized. Here it is a disembodied voice above a cloud of darkness in a prison, and it says it three times. The second half of the voice's sentence — 'and seek no more to destroy my servants' — has no Matthean counterpart and is what the borrowing is for: the forerunner's summons is being addressed to men in the act of attempted murder.

5:32.note: A verbatim eight-word reproduction of a KJV verse, and the highest-scoring machine candidate in the chapter (rarity 2.86, ten-word run) — one of the rare cases where the n-gram stream ranks the true source first. Note that the same clause is already adjudicated at Alma 9:25 and 10:20; it is written again because Helaman is a new book and because the voice, unlike Alma's preachers, is not quoting a prophet but is itself the speaker.
5:32.text: And saying, Repent ye: for the kingdom of heaven is at hand.

provenance.route: Romans 8:26 + 2 Corinthians 12:4 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “cannot be uttered” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Romans 8:26, of the Spirit's 'groanings which cannot be uttered'. “not lawful for a man to utter” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Corinthians 12:4, of what Paul heard in paradise. Helaman 5:33's 'marvellous words, which cannot be uttered by man' has the first phrase and the second phrase's agent.
provenance.significance: The KJV has two things that cannot be uttered and they are opposite. Romans 8:26's are groans without words, uttered by the Spirit because the believer does not know what to pray for; 2 Corinthians 12:4's are words too holy to repeat, heard by a man caught up into paradise. Helaman 5:33 fuses them into a third thing — 'marvellous words, which cannot be uttered by man' — which takes Romans' impossibility and applies it to Paul's content. The result is a definition the KJV does not contain: not inarticulate, and not forbidden, but beyond human articulation. That fusion is also what the chapter needs, because twelve verses later the same men 'could speak forth marvellous words' (5:45), so the unutterable becomes utterable once the Holy Spirit has come down.

5:33.note: Two KJV singletons, from two epistles, joined in one clause. Neither alone would carry the link — 'cannot be uttered' is four common words and Romans' context is prayer, not theophany — but the pairing is the evidence: the Book of Mormon has the phrase from one verse and the agent from the other, and the two verses are the KJV's only statements about speech that cannot be produced.
5:33.whyNot: Both phrases are short and idiomatic, and 'which cannot be uttered by man' is available to any nineteenth-century writer describing a revelation. If only Romans 8:26 were in view the sense would be wrong, since Paul's groanings are wordless and Helaman's are words.
5:33.text: Likewise the Spirit also helpeth our infirmities: for we know not what we should pray for as we ought: but the Spirit itself maketh intercession for us with groanings which cannot be uttered.

provenance.other: “the face of an angel” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Helaman 5:36 has the plural, 'even as the face of angels', because there are two prisoners. Matthew 17:2's transfiguration reads 'his face did shine as the sun' and Exodus 34:29 has Moses' skin shining, but neither has the comparison to an angel.
provenance.significance: Acts 6:15 is Stephen before the council, and it is the last thing said about him before the speech that gets him killed; Acts 7:55-56 completes it — he looks up stedfastly into heaven, sees the heavens opened, and says so, and they stone him. Helaman 5:36 gives a dissenter the same sight from the wrong side of it: he 'saw through the cloud of darkness the faces of Nephi and Lehi; and behold, they did shine exceedingly, even as the face of angels. And he beheld that they did lift their eyes to Heaven.' That is Acts 6:15 and Acts 7:55 in Luke's order, seen by a man standing where the council stood. Twelve verses later the borrowing completes itself at 5:48: 'they saw the heavens open'. What Acts makes the prelude to a lynching, Helaman makes the prelude to a mass conversion — the council's own vision, given to the council, and believed.

5:36.note: A KJV singleton pluralized, in the middle of a sustained reworking of Acts 6-7. Adjudicated at Mosiah 13:5 (Abinadi before Noah's priests) and written again here because Helaman is a new book and because this occurrence is embedded in the Stephen sequence rather than standing alone: the shining face, the lifted eyes, and the opened heaven arrive in Luke's own order across 5:36-48.
5:36.text: And all that sat in the council, looking stedfastly on him, saw his face as it had been the face of an angel.

provenance.other: “what shall we do” occurs in exactly twelve KJV verses and is no evidence on its own; “when they heard this” occurs in exactly three, of which Acts 2:37 is one. The n-gram stream ranked John 6:28 here on a seven-word run, 'unto him, What shall we do, that', which is a closer string match than Acts 2:37. It is the wrong verse: John 6:28's question is 'that we might work the works of God', asked of Jesus by a crowd looking for a sign, and nothing else in Helaman 5 touches John 6. Acts 2:37's 'what shall we do' is followed by 'Repent, and be baptized', which is Aminadab's answer at 5:41; and Acts 2:37's opening, 'Now when they heard this', is reproduced word for word at Helaman 5:48, 'And now when they heard this'.
provenance.significance: Helaman 5:38-48 is a Pentecost. The crowd asks what they must do, is told to repent, cries out, and the Holy Spirit comes down from heaven and fills them with fire so that they speak marvellous words (5:45) — which is Acts 2:2-4 in Acts' order. What the borrowing does is relocate Pentecost inside a jail and give it to the wrong audience: Acts' crowd are devout Jews out of every nation, Helaman's are Lamanite soldiers and Nephite dissenters who came to commit a murder. Acts 2:37's crowd are 'pricked in their heart'; Helaman's are held immovable by fear in a cloud of darkness, which is the same conviction rendered as a physical restraint.

5:40.note: 'What shall we do, that this cloud of darkness may be removed from overshadowing us?' The question is Acts 2:37's, and the answer at 5:41 is Acts 2:38's — 'You must repent'. Written at 5:40 because that is where the wording starts; the Pentecost frame it opens is carried by the separate link at 5:45. The machine's higher-scoring John 6:28 is excluded (see the register).
5:40.text: Now when they heard this, they were pricked in their heart, and said unto Peter and to the rest of the apostles, Men and brethren, what shall we do?

provenance.other: “unspeakable and full of glory” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The Book of Mormon reads 'that joy which is unspeakable and full of glory' against Peter's 'ye rejoice with joy unspeakable and full of glory' — five words verbatim, with the noun moved in front of a relative clause. This is well below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and is catalogued as a quotation on the rarity, per CONVENTIONS §2.
provenance.significance: 1 Peter 1:8's joy belongs to people who have not seen Christ: 'whom having not seen, ye love; in whom, though now ye see him not, yet believing, ye rejoice with joy unspeakable and full of glory.' Helaman 5:44 gives it to men who are at that moment inside a pillar of fire, being ministered to by angels, four verses before they see the heavens open. The borrowing therefore says the opposite of its source about sight, and the preceding verse of Peter says why the phrase was reachable at all: 1 Peter 1:7 is about faith 'tried with fire', which is the literal condition of the men in this verse. The fire that tries the faith and the joy that follows are Peter's two images in sequence, and Helaman has put a man inside the first one.

5:44.note: Five words of a KJV singleton, reproduced exactly. The chapter has already borrowed from 1 Peter at 5:8 ('fadeth not away'), which makes the epistle a live source here rather than a coincidence, and 1 Peter 1:7's trial by fire stands immediately before the borrowed clause in Peter and immediately around the speaker in Helaman.
5:44.text: Whom having not seen, ye love; in whom, though now ye see him not, yet believing, ye rejoice with joy unspeakable and full of glory:

provenance.other: “cloven tongues” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and the Book of Mormon does not have it, which is why this is an extended allusion and not a quotation. What it has is Acts' sequence: a coming down from heaven, a filling, fire, and speech. The n-gram stream matched 'the holy Spirit of God' to Ephesians 4:30, which is the KJV's phrasing ('grieve not the holy Spirit of God') and is probably where the exact wording comes from; the scene is Acts'. The 1830 spells 'marvellous', preserving the KJV orthography that 1920 dropped (CONVENTIONS §8).
provenance.significance: Acts 2:2-4 has a sound from heaven, fire that sits on each of them, all filled with the Holy Ghost, and speech in other tongues 'as the Spirit gave them utterance'. Helaman 5:45 has the Holy Spirit come down from heaven, enter into their hearts, fill them 'as if with fire', and enable them to 'speak forth marvellous words'. Every element is present and every one is softened by an 'as if', which is this chapter's habit — the fire is as if, the whisper is as if, the walls are as if about to tumble. Acts 2:11 calls what the Pentecost crowd heard 'the wonderful works of God'; Helaman calls it marvellous words, and twelve verses earlier (5:33) the same words were the ones that 'cannot be uttered by man'. The Spirit's arrival is what makes them sayable.

5:45.note: The completion of the Acts 2 frame opened at 5:40. No phrase of Acts is reproduced — the wording of 'the Holy Spirit of God' is Ephesians 4:30's — but the four events of Pentecost arrive in Pentecost's order in a single sentence, and the chapter's own earlier verses supply the two ends of it: the crowd's 'what shall we do' at 5:40 and the unutterable words at 5:33.
5:45.whyNot: Entirely structural. A writer describing an outpouring of the Spirit in nineteenth-century English would reach for descent from heaven, fire and inspired speech without needing Acts 2 in front of him, and the one KJV singleton in the neighbourhood, 'cloven tongues', is absent.
5:45.text: And there appeared unto them cloven tongues like as of fire, and it sat upon each of them.

provenance.other: “peace be unto you” occurs in exactly four KJV verses — Luke 24:36, John 20:19, 20:21 and 20:26 — and all four are the risen Christ appearing to disciples, twice with the doors expressly shut. The doubling, 'Peace, peace', is Isaiah 26:3's and Jeremiah 6:14's Hebraism and is not from John. “from the foundation of the world” occurs in six KJV verses; the one that joins it to a beloved son is Revelation 13:8's Lamb slain from the foundation of the world.
provenance.significance: The four KJV 'Peace be unto you' verses are the resurrection appearances, and two of them make a point of the shut doors: Jesus is inside a room the disciples had locked for fear. Helaman 5:47 gives the greeting to men inside a prison whose walls have just been described as standing — 'neither did it take hold upon the walls of the prison' (5:44). The salutation therefore arrives exactly where John puts it, in a sealed room, and the speaker is unseen. Jeremiah 6:14's 'Peace, peace; when there is no peace' is the doubling's other home and is the ironic reading the passage does not take.

5:47.note: 'Peace, peace be unto you, because of your faith in my well beloved, which was from the foundation of the world.' Held at moderate: the greeting is four words available from four verses, and the doubling comes from elsewhere. What argues for John is the setting — the KJV's peace-greeting is spoken to people shut in a room, and this one is spoken to people shut in a prison — and what fills out the sentence is Revelation 13:8's clause, which supplies the two things the KJV never says of anyone else, that he is the beloved and that he was from the foundation of the world.
5:47.whyNot: 'Peace be unto you' is a formula available from four KJV verses and from ordinary devotional English, and the second half of the sentence is a different source; nothing in the verse is reproduced at more than four consecutive words.
5:47.text: Then the same day at evening, being the first day of the week, when the doors were shut where the disciples were assembled for fear of the Jews, came Jesus and stood in the midst, and saith unto them, Peace be unto you.
